question: Can a small causal sequence decoder serve as a general numeric output head for an arbitrary feature encoder, matching conventional point and histogram heads while also representing flexible one-dimensional conditional densities?

key_findings.claim: The proposed head separates input representation from numeric output representation and autoregressively decodes a constrained token sequence into one real value.
key_findings.evidence: A feature encoder supplies the initial context to a compact Transformer. Normalized targets use a base-B fractional expansion, while unnormalized targets use sign, exponent-sign, exponent-digit, and mantissa-digit tokens; position-specific masking permits only valid numeric tokens. The default small head can be one layer with 32 units and one attention head, less than 10% of the full network in the reported experiments.

anchors.section: 3 Decoding-Based Regression and 3.1 Numeric Token Representations

key_findings.claim: Under K-bit universality and exact maximum-likelihood fitting, every prefix length of the normalized binary decoder is a conventional equal-width histogram estimator.
key_findings.evidence: The proof identifies the fitted K-bit distribution with empirical bin frequencies and obtains all shorter-prefix distributions by marginalization. It then gives the familiar asymptotic integrated-risk tradeoff: a 2^(-2k) derivative-dependent bias term and a 2^k/N variance term, with lower-order remainder terms.

key_findings.claim: The theorem does not itself explain a finite Transformer decoder's apparent low-sample regularization, and its wording is stronger than the derivation supports.
key_findings.evidence: Universality plus exact empirical maximum likelihood makes the decoder exactly the histogram whose variance the experiment says the trained decoder avoids. The manuscript therefore attributes the gap at N=1024 and large K to an unproved combination of model and SGD bias. The displayed result is an asymptotic expansion with big-O terms, despite being introduced as an exact computation for all k up to K; the proof also promotes a total O(epsilon^4) squared-bias remainder from only C2 smoothness by treating a point-dependent Taylor remainder as though its odd cross term cancels exactly. Softmax probabilities additionally approach, rather than attain at finite logits, empirical distributions containing zero-count bins.

anchors.section: B Histogram reduction and bias analysis

key_findings.claim: Both normalized and unnormalized decoder heads are competitive with ordinary point heads across the paper's synthetic and real tabular regression settings.
key_findings.evidence: On BBOB functions with about 100,000 training examples, mean Kendall tau is nearly tied across heads from 5 to 20 dimensions: for example, at dimension 5 the unnormalized decoder, normalized decoder, pointwise head, and Riemann head score 89.56, 89.40, 89.08, and 88.94. Across AMLB and OpenML-CTR23 tasks with at most 10,000 training examples and 10 runs per bar, the decoder wins a majority of paired task comparisons against the point head and usually beats the Riemann head. Data-scaling panels show the normalized decoder reaching lower relative MSE than the histogram on nearly every AMLB task, although the paper reports plots rather than a pooled uncertainty test.

key_findings.claim: Autoregressive numeric heads model non-Gaussian conditional densities more reliably than the tested histogram and mixture-density baselines, but decoded outliers remain visible.
key_findings.evidence: Rendered samples recover half-moon, zig-zag, spiral, and hollow-square conditional shapes. Across 25 UCI datasets and 10 train-test splits, both decoder variants have average NLL below 0.70 on every listed dataset; the Riemann head is worse on every row, while the mixture-density network ranges from strong negative NLL to catastrophic values such as 7.49 on Kin40K and 7.09 on Slice. Vanilla temperature near 1 best preserves the displayed density shapes, while lower temperature and top-k/top-p filtering trade noise for bias.

anchors.section: A.5 Full UCI Density Estimation Results

key_findings.claim: Sequence design materially changes point-estimation error: repeated token blocks with majority voting reduce extreme-sample failures, whereas a Hamming-distance code does not help.
key_findings.evidence: For the unnormalized decoder with sample-mean aggregation, ordinary decoding becomes worse as more samples increase the chance of a gross exponent error. Repeating the numeric sequence and majority-voting each position substantially lowers relative MSE, with too many repeats again becoming difficult to learn. A separate nine-task ablation finds the proposed Hamming-distance representation usually no better, and often worse, than the binary tree representation.

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence is broad at small tabular scale but does not validate modern language-model regression, calibrated predictive uncertainty, or multivariate outputs.
key_findings.evidence: Experiments share a tuned MLP encoder and mostly a one-layer 32-unit decoder, use early stopping and per-head hyperparameter sweeps, and evaluate single scalar targets. The discussion explicitly excludes real LLM tokenizers, mixed language-and-number outputs, RL training, multi-objective regression, and more complex stochastic regression architectures. Density quality is assessed by NLL and visual sampling without calibration, coverage, or proper-scoring comparisons beyond likelihood.

method.core_idea: Replace a scalar or parametric distribution head with a small constrained autoregressive decoder whose token prefixes recursively refine a numeric interval.
method.mechanism: Encode each target as either a fixed-length base-B fractional expansion or a floating-point-like sign/exponent/mantissa sequence, train every token with teacher-forced cross-entropy, constrain valid tokens by position at inference, and turn the resulting sequence distribution into a point estimate by sampling or into a discrete density over decoded values.
assumptions: The target is a single real scalar within the representable range and the chosen precision makes rounding error acceptable.
Training examples are sufficient to learn positional significance and autoregressive dependencies without numeric pretraining.
Target normalization bounds are available when the normalized vocabulary is used and transfer safely to test data.
A tuned sampling or aggregation rule returns the decision statistic required by the downstream loss.
The theoretical histogram reduction assumes exact maximum-likelihood fitting by a K-bit-universal model; the empirical Transformer is not shown to satisfy this premise.
The shared MLP encoder and per-head sweeps provide a fair comparison for the selected tabular tasks.

techniques.role: Autoregressively represents a scalar predictive distribution using a small token decoder attached to any feature vector.
Maps normalized targets to a hierarchical base-B partition whose prefixes form progressively finer histograms.
Extends the numeric range with sign, exponent, and mantissa tokens when target normalization is undesirable.
Masks invalid token types at each numeric position so every generated sequence parses as a supported real value.
Converts the learned sequence distribution to means, medians, or modes chosen for the evaluation loss.
Repeats the numeric token block during training and majority-votes corresponding positions to suppress rare high-significance errors.

evaluations.setting: One-dimensional synthetic functions and 5-20 dimensional BBOB objectives with approximately 100,000 training points
evaluations.metric: Visual function fit and Kendall-tau correlation averaged over 10 runs
evaluations.result: Both decoder heads track difficult scales and discontinuities and are broadly tied with point and Riemann heads on aggregate BBOB correlation
evaluations.baseline: Pointwise MLP and Riemann histogram heads

evaluations.setting: AMLB and OpenML-CTR23 real-world tabular tasks with at most 10,000 training points
evaluations.metric: Kendall tau and relative MSE, with 10-run averages
evaluations.result: Decoder heads are competitive with pointwise heads, win a majority of displayed task pairs, and generally dominate the Riemann head
evaluations.baseline: Tuned pointwise and Riemann heads sharing the same encoder

evaluations.setting: AMLB training-set scaling from roughly 10 to 10,000 examples
evaluations.metric: Relative MSE averaged over 10 resampled training runs
evaluations.result: The normalized decoder usually improves beyond the histogram plateau and sometimes remains better than the point head in both low- and high-data regimes

evaluations.setting: Twenty-five UCI conditional-density datasets over 10 train-test splits
evaluations.metric: Average test negative log likelihood with split standard deviation
evaluations.result: Both decoders remain below 0.70 NLL on every listed dataset; Riemann is worse in all rows, while MDN alternates between the best result and severe failure
evaluations.baseline: Mixture-density network and Riemann histogram heads

evaluations.metric: Rendered sample fit to the ground-truth support and density
evaluations.result: Vanilla temperature sampling best preserves the multimodal shapes; lower temperature, top-p, and top-k introduce visible bias, and every method exhibits some sample noise
evaluations.baseline: Mixture-density network, Riemann head, and alternate decoder sampling rules

evaluations.setting: AMLB decoder-size, sample-count, repetition-code, and Hamming-code ablations
evaluations.metric: UCI NLL or relative MSE over 10 training runs
evaluations.result: Moderate decoder capacity is sufficient, token repetition reduces sample-mean outliers, and Hamming-distance tokenization does not improve the default tree code
evaluations.baseline: Default decoder size, no repetition, and ordinary binary tree tokenization

limitations: The density theorem reduces an ideal universal decoder to a histogram; it neither proves the finite Transformer's implicit regularization nor justifies the phrase 'exactly computed' for an asymptotic expansion.
The stated C2 smoothness is not clearly sufficient for the proof's O(2^(-4k)) integrated squared-bias remainder, whose Taylor cross-term cancellation is asserted rather than established.
All experimental targets are scalar; multi-output dependence is proposed but not tested.
The controlled decoder uses ideal digit tokens and constrained decoding rather than a pretrained language model's tokenizer, intermediate prose, or instruction-tuning dynamics.
Point predictions depend on a tuned sampling/aggregation rule and can be unstable under rare exponent-token errors.
The normalized vocabulary relies on training-set min/max bounds and can clip or extrapolate poorly under target shift.
Most comparisons use small tabular MLP systems and omit tree ensembles, quantile methods, flows, stochastic neural regressors, and calibrated uncertainty baselines.

The released code directory implements the decoder and vocabularies with one basic end-to-end test, but does not include the paper's dataset pipelines, sweep configurations, figure scripts, or full reproduction harness.
failure_modes: A single wrong sign or exponent token can create an extreme decoded outlier and corrupt sample means.
Increasing vocabulary base, precision, or repetition length can make token dependencies too data-hungry for the available sample size.
Top-k, top-p, or low-temperature sampling can suppress genuine modes while trying to remove numerical noise.
Training-set min/max normalization can map shifted test targets outside the representable interval.
Teacher forcing can hide exposure errors that accumulate when multiple numeric outputs or interleaved language must be generated autoregressively.
A more expressive decoder can overfit, and larger head sizes do not monotonically improve UCI NLL.
A likelihood-competitive discrete density can still be poorly calibrated or yield a poor point action for the downstream loss.
reusable_insights: Factor the input encoder and output distribution head when testing whether token generation itself adds value.
A radix tree converts exponential output resolution into a small vocabulary plus sequence depth and supplies useful coarse-to-fine prefix marginals.
Choose the point estimator from the evaluation loss rather than treating one autoregressive sample as the prediction.
Audit high-significance token errors separately from ordinary residual error; repetition can be useful when failures are sparse and positional.
Compare a learned hierarchical decoder with an equal-resolution flat histogram to expose the data-efficiency effect of shared prefixes.
Treat a universal-model theorem and the practical model's implicit bias as separate claims when the theorem collapses the model to a classical estimator.
open_questions: Can a finite-capacity theory characterize the decoder and optimizer bias that produces lower variance than the ideal empirical histogram?
Which numeric code minimizes expected downstream loss under realistic token errors, target ranges, and decoding budgets?
Do the gains survive pretrained language-model tokenizers, mixed rationale-and-number outputs, and reinforcement learning?
How should predictive means, quantiles, and calibrated intervals be computed without costly or heavy-tailed autoregressive sampling?
Can hierarchical decoding model multivariate targets competitively without making ordering choices and exposure bias dominant?
How do decoder heads compare with conditional flows, distribution-free sample networks, quantile regression, and conformal prediction under matched compute and calibration metrics?
Does sequence-level numeric supervision or regression-aware token loss remove the observed need for repetition and sampling heuristics?

competitive_landscape.title: OmniPred: Language Models as Universal Regressors
competitive_landscape.difference: OmniPred trains one language model across heterogeneous black-box optimization tasks with both inputs and scalar outputs serialized as text. Decoding-based Regression isolates the output side by attaching a tiny decoder to a fixed feature representation, adds normalized and floating-point vocabularies, compares ordinary heads, and studies conditional density estimation rather than cross-task transfer.

competitive_landscape.title: From Words to Numbers: Your Large Language Model Is Secretly A Capable Regressor When Given In-Context Examples
competitive_landscape.difference: Vacareanu et al. prompt pretrained service and open models with regression examples and study regret without gradient updates. The target instead trains a small numeric head from scratch on arbitrary encoder features and attributes data efficiency to hierarchical output representation; it does not test pretrained in-context reasoning.

competitive_landscape.title: Regression Aware Inference with LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Lukasik et al. show that ordinary autoregressive samples are suboptimal for regression metrics and estimate Bayes-optimal decisions from an LLM's generated responses. The target cites this point-estimation principle but focuses on the head's representation, histogram risk, and density fit; its sampling and aggregation rule remains a tuned application choice.

competitive_landscape.title: Better autoregressive regression with LLMs via regression-aware fine-tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: RAFT derives a Bayes-optimal regression-aware fine-tuning loss for decoder LLMs and compares autoregressive and predictive-head approaches across natural-language regression benchmarks. Decoding-based Regression keeps standard token cross-entropy, isolates a lightweight numeric head on tabular encoders, and uniquely evaluates arbitrary one-dimensional densities and hierarchical histogram risk.

competitive_landscape.title: Regress, Don't Guess: A Regression-like Loss on Number Tokens for Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Number Token Loss augments cross-entropy with Lp- or Wasserstein-based distance between numeric token values, improves arithmetic, matches a regression head on one regression task, and scales to 3B parameters without inference overhead. It directly addresses the nominal-token-loss weakness that the target accepts and tries to overcome through hierarchical coding and data.

competitive_landscape.title: Beyond Token-level Supervision: Unlocking the Potential of Decoding-based Regression via Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. explicitly build on decoding-based regression and replace purely token-level supervision with sequence-level numerical rewards optimized by ReMax or GRPO. They report gains over token-loss and traditional heads on tabular and code-metric regression, narrowing the target's claim that ordinary cross-entropy plus representation design is sufficient for highest precision.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first focused study of autoregressive numeric output heads independent of text inputs, formalizes normalized and unnormalized numeric codes, derives density-estimation risk, and shows a tiny cross-entropy-trained decoder can match point heads while outperforming flat histograms and mixture-density heads.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The 28-page TMLR version gives a clean encoder/head factorization, two numeric vocabularies, constrained decoding and point-estimation choices, a histogram-risk derivation, synthetic and real regression tests, 25 UCI density tasks, size and sampling ablations, repetition coding, a negative Hamming-code result, and exact hyperparameter grids.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the controlled treatment of a causal numeric sequence model as a swap-in output distribution head, together with the hierarchical flat-histogram comparison and unusually broad scalar density experiments. It is not a general proof that practical decoder heads are universal or implicitly regularized: under its strongest premise the head is exactly the empirical histogram, while the favorable finite-model gap is conjectural and the theorem's remainder is overstated. Prior text-to-text and Bayes-decision work already established autoregressive regression; contemporary RAFT and later Number Token Loss and sequence-level RL show that loss alignment, not tokenization alone, remains an active and often stronger lever. The supported claim is therefore a useful, flexible scalar head at small tabular scale, not the definitive regression interface for modern LLMs.
